title: Kentucky’s Proposed Social Studies Standards Need More Work
author: Gary Houchens
summary: Gary Houchens, a Western Kentucky University professor of educational leadership and former member of the Kentucky Board of Education, publishes the public comment he submitted on the state's proposed 2026 social studies standards. He recalls welcoming the more coherent 2018 standards but now judges that Kentucky's standards have been too vague for too long. His evidence is the 2026 assessment results, in which only about a third of students at any grade level are proficient, together with wider gaps in public historical and civic knowledge. He argues that without explicit statements of what students should know in history, geography, government and economics, teachers cannot choose curricular materials or assess well and are effectively guessing what the state test will cover. The draft is the best yet, he concedes, but still far thinner than Massachusetts, so he endorses colleague Richard Innes's critique and asks the board to return the draft to the drafting committee.
points: Houchens ties low social studies proficiency, about a third of students, to decades of insufficiently specific state standards rather than to teacher effort.
Vague standards leave teachers guessing what the state assessment will ask, which undermines both curriculum selection and the meaning of test results.
He benchmarks Kentucky against Massachusetts and the Civics Alliance's American Birthright model as examples of knowledge-specific standards.
The piece shows a credible insider changing his mind about standards he once championed, and it models a concise public comment with a clear ask.
quotes: As a member of KBE, I was delighted when in 2018 KDE proposed new social studies standards that were more coherent and specific than any I had previously seen throughout my career.

The 2026 Kentucky assessment results indicate that only about a third of students at any grade level are proficient in social studies standards. Other publicly available data reveal major gaps in historic and civic knowledge on the part of the general population.
I believe the lack of social science knowledge and understanding is directly related to decades of insufficiently specific state-level standards.

Without comprehensive standards that explicitly describe what students should know about history, geography, government, and economics, teachers are at a loss for how to select appropriate curricular materials or assess student performance.
They are literally guessing as to what students will be asked on the annual statewide assessment, and those assessment results may not even accurately convey what students have learned.
The proposed 2026 standards are the best we’ve seen so far but still are far less comprehensive than other states like Massachusetts.

These frameworks make clear that even with its standards improvements, Kentucky has as long way to go in terms of its expectations for robust, specific, and measurable knowledge of social studies skills and concepts.
